title: Hannah Senesh
hookLine: a young poet and paratrooper who went back into occupied Europe

cards: A beach at Caesarea, on the coast of the land of Israel. A young woman who grew up in Budapest walks along the sand and writes a short poem.

In it, she asks that some things never end: the sand and the sea, the rustle of the water, the lightning of the sky, the prayer of a human being. Set to music, it's sung in Israel as Eli, Eli. My God, my God.
Its title calls it a walk to Caesarea. Not long after, she volunteered to go back into the war that had swallowed her family's Europe.

teach.h: BUDAPEST, A DIARY, A KIBBUTZ BY THE SEA.
teach.b: Hannah Senesh grew up in a Jewish family in Budapest, writing poems and keeping a diary from girlhood. As a young woman she moved to the land of Israel and lived on a kibbutz by the sea called Sdot Yam.
Then the news from Europe grew darker.
She joined a small group of Jewish volunteers from the land, trained by the British army, who parachuted into occupied Europe to help the Allies and to reach Jews wherever they could.
She came down in Yugoslavia and crossed toward Hungary, where her mother still lived.
She was captured at the border. In prison she was beaten and questioned, and the story told about her is that she would not give up her radio code. Her mother, arrested too, saw her there.
Hannah was tried and shot by a firing squad, still a young woman. Before she crossed the border, she handed a fellow volunteer a short poem.

In it she blesses a match, used up in lighting a flame. She blesses the flame too, and a heart that knows when to stop beating, for the sake of honor. That's a paraphrase; the Hebrew is spare and plain.
Notice where she begins and ends: not with the fire, with the match. A match has one job. It burns itself out so that something else can catch.
Some remember her as a fighter, some first as a poet, and some find both in the same few lines.

how: Hannah Senesh's poems are read and sung in Israel, especially Eli, Eli (A Walk to Caesarea) and the match poem, and she is remembered at memorial gatherings and in schools.

games.q: you're Hannah, safe on a kibbutz by the sea, while the news from Europe grows darker. a mission is forming. what do you do?

practice: Take the beach poem, in paraphrase, one piece at a time: the sand and the sea, the rustle of the water, the lightning of the sky, the prayer of a human being.

Say each one slowly, leaving a whole breath between them, then rest on the last. If you pray, let her words carry your prayer for a while; if not, let them be a short list of things you'd like never to end.
